newsitem.title: UK: FOCUS-Tate optimistic for medium term.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-Tate optimistic for medium term.

text.p: International sweetener group Tate & Lyle Plc, which saw first half profits plunge, said on Wednesday cost cuts would help its medium term performance, but was cautious about an upturn in its U.S. fructose business.
Profits were squeezed by margin pressures at Tate's A.E. Staley sweetener business in North America. And the strength of sterling reduced overall earnings by 17.3 million pounds ($28.3 million) .
Tate's shares were three pence lower at 451 pence after the group reported first half profits before tax and exceptional costs of 113.6 million pounds, down from 168.2 million last time.
Chairman Sir Neil Shaw said the group expected improved returns from North American starch and sweetener operations in the second half.
He said Tate's Staley would perform well relative to its competitors and sugar operations should continue to make good progress.
"The outturn for the second half of the year will benefit from these improvements but is likely to be affected by the continued strength of sterling," he said in a statement.
The company said structural problems in the U.S. fructose business could be past their worst days, but the position would remain unclear until contracts were negotiated towards the year end.
Chief executive Larry Pillard said it seemed as though the fructose market could be bottoming out based on overall capacity utilisation.
"Some of the capacity utilisation we see would tend to make you believe we're on the upswing of the cycle," he told Reuters.
Unsustainably high capacity utilisation in 1994/95 led to high margins which drew a lot of capital investment into the fructose side of the business, he said.
High fructose corn syrup, produced by Staley, is used as a sweetener in soft drinks like Coca Cola and Pepsi.
Pillard, who took over as chief executive in November last year, has undertaken a major review of the group, which has included asset write-downs of certain underperforming businesses.
In North America this produced an exceptional charge of 29.9 million pounds. The group expects payback over two years, Pillard said.
The chief executive said there had also been strong cost initiatives in other parts of the group and management had been refocused on improving returns for investors.
"I think we're refocused as management on performance and we're working very diligently to make sure that we assure shareholder returns."
Cost cutting had benefited the group's North American sugar business. The group was optimistic that good underlying growth and supply, plus cost cuts would sustain its strong performance.
In Europe, overcapacity in potato starch had put pressure on some of the starch markets and there was tough competition in other sweetener products.
The strong pound reduced profits in Europe by 11.8 million pounds, including 6.4 million at Tate & Lyle Sugars due to the revaluation of the "Green Pound."
But Pillard said the biggest factor in Europe had been start up costs associated with its reorganisation of its production in Europe.

"The main thrusts of those starts ups will continue through this calendar year," he said, predicting that the group should see returns from the investment flowing through in the last half of 1998. ($ = 0.611 British Pounds)
